newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll shows east Germans sceptical over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows east Germans sceptical over EMU.

text.p: Most eastern Germans, who only got the deutschemark in 1990, either oppose scrapping the German currency under European monetary union (EMU) or want the single currency to be delayed, a poll showed on Friday.
The survey, in the Saechsischer Zeitung newspaper, found that just six percent of people living in formerly communist eastern Germany wanted the euro to be launched on time in 1999.
Half of a sample of 1,200 people polled by the Leipzig Institut fuer Marktforschung called for a delay to the single currency project, while a third opposed EMU altogether.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl vowed recently that EMU would go ahead on schedule with Germany meeting the tough fiscal criteria set by the Maastricht treaty. Polls regularly show, however, that the German public does not share his enthusiasm for abandoning the traditionally stable mark.

The east German poll did not give a precise breakdown. But it noted that young east Germans opposed the single currency most strongly. Forty-three percent of 18- to 29-year-olds said the euro project should be abandoned altogether.
Supporters of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrat party (CDU) had a more favourable attitude, with 11 percent favouring a prompt launch of the euro and 23 percent flatly opposing EMU.
Hopes that the single currency will have beneficial effects have also shrunk, with just 11 percent saying EMU would be positive for Germany -- down from 15 percent last December.
Fifty-one percent, however, expect there to be negative consequences, up from 49 percent. Some 29 percent said the euro would be neither negative nor positive.
